title: Standing at the Grave
subtitle: On officiating a funeral, preaching to the grieving, and telling the truth about death in the presence of hope

sections.title: When the Call Comes
sections.body:
The phone rings and someone is gone. Now a family who can barely think is looking to you to carry them through the worst week of their lives, and the funeral is in four days, and you have a sermon to write and a casket to stand beside and no idea yet what you will say.

Go to them first. Before you write a word, go.

Sit in the house where the absence is loudest. Let them talk about the one who died. Ask them to tell you stories, the funny ones and the hard ones, and write the details down, because those details are the bricks you will build the service from and grief will steal them from the family if no one writes them down. You are not gathering material for a performance. You are gathering a life, and you are telling a shattered family that this person mattered enough to be remembered truly. I have walked into those houses dreading them and walked out having received more than I gave. The grieving will preach to you, if you let them, about what actually lasts.

sections.title: Tell the Truth About Death
sections.body:
Do not stand at a grave and lie. The grieving can smell it, and a lie told over a coffin does damage that lasts for years.

Death is not a natural part of the circle of life. Death is an enemy. Scripture calls it the last enemy, and the body in that box is the proof.

We have built an entire industry to soften this. He is not really gone. She is in a better place watching over us. He just stepped into the next room. Some of that is true in the end, and all of it is poison when it is offered too soon, because it tells a weeping daughter that her tears are an overreaction to a thing that is basically fine. It is not fine. The God who stood at the tomb of his friend Lazarus, who knew he was about to raise him, wept anyway. He did not lecture the sisters about the resurrection while they were sobbing. He wept. If the Son of God will weep at a grave, you can stop pretending and weep at one too. Name the loss as loss. Say the word died. Only the funeral that tells the truth about death has earned the right to speak about hope, and the hope offered to people who have not been allowed to grieve is a hope they cannot believe.

sections.title: Preaching to the Grieving
sections.body:
Now build the message, and build it for the people actually in the room, most of whom are not in church and many of whom are furious at God or convinced he is not there.

Keep it short. A funeral sermon that runs long is a sermon that has forgotten who it is for.

Name the person. Use their name, tell a true story, let the room laugh once if the life held laughter, because honest remembering is part of the healing and a service that could be about anyone is about no one. Then turn, not with a clever pivot but with the plain weight of the gospel, to the only thing that holds at a graveside. Not that the deceased was a good person, because that is a thin reed and everyone in the room over forty knows it will not hold their weight. Turn to Christ. Turn to a tomb that could not keep him, to a promise that those who are his will rise as he rose, to a God who entered death himself so that death would not have the last word over those he loves. Do not promise what you do not know about where this particular soul has gone. Preach the hope that is sure for all who are in Christ, and let God handle the secret things. Aim the whole sermon at the living, because the dead are past your help and the living are sitting in front of you wondering whether any of this is true.

sections.title: The Funeral of a Child
sections.body:
And then there is the one you pray never comes, and it comes. The small casket. The parents who will never be the same people again. The room where no one believes in any kind of order at all.

Here you must say less and weep more. The temptation to explain is a temptation to wound.

Do not tell these parents that God needed another angel, because he did not, and angels are not dead children, and you have just made God the thief who took their daughter. Do not tell them everything happens for a reason and then leave them to imagine what reason could possibly be worth this. There is no reason you can offer that will not be an insult. So offer something else. Offer the God who lost a son himself, who knows from the inside what a Father feels when a child dies, who did not stay safely above the suffering but came down into the middle of it. Offer the smallest, surest words. Jesus took the children in his arms. Jesus called the little ones to himself and was indignant at anyone who kept them away. Stand with the parents in the rubble and do not try to rebuild the house that day. Some funerals are not for explaining. They are only for accompanying. I have done this, and I had almost nothing to say, and what I had I said quietly, and quiet was the only honest volume in that room.

sections.kicker: The Work That Outlasts the Service
sections.title: After the Grave
sections.body:
The casseroles stop coming. The cards stop. Three weeks after the funeral the world has moved on, and the widow is sitting alone in a house that is too quiet for the first time, and that is when grief actually arrives.

The funeral is not the end of your work. It is the start of it.

Mark your calendar for the months no one else will remember. The first birthday without them. The first Christmas. The anniversary of the death, which the grieving dread and the rest of us forget. A phone call on those days, a visit, a simple I have not forgotten, will mean more than the entire funeral, because anyone will show up the week of a death and almost no one shows up the season after. This is shepherding in its plainest form. You buried someone they loved, and now you walk the long road of their grief beside them, not to hurry it, not to fix it, only to keep them company until the Lord does the healing that you cannot. That is the ministry. It does not end at the grave. It begins there.
